item.title: WATCH: GOP holdout rejects Trump threat as AG nominee standoff explodes
item.description: Thom Tillis dismissed Trump's threat to withdraw Todd Blanche's nomination for attorney general, saying the White House must honor a prior commitment.
item.content:encoded:
Sen. Thom Tillis, R-N.C., brushed aside President Donald Trump's threat to withdraw acting Attorney General Todd Blanche's nomination Thursday, arguing the White House must instead honor what he says was an earlier commitment to win his vote.

"That's his prerogative," Tillis said of Trump’s threat to withdraw Blanche’s nomination.

Tillis’ comments come after Trump called out both Tillis and Sen. John Cornyn, R-Texas, on Truth Social Thursday morning for blocking the president’s efforts to make Blanche the nation’s top prosecutor. 

Trump then threatened to pull Blanche’s nomination until the two Republican senators leave office next year. Tillis is retiring, and Cornyn lost his primary in his run for re-election.

TRUMP THREATENS TO YANK HIS OWN AG NOMINEE AS GOP REVOLT GROWS

Tillis argued Trump cannot resolve this nomination standoff "unless we fulfill what we thought was the commitment from the administration."

The North Carolina senator has withheld his support for Blanche unless the administration agrees to permanently eliminate the nearly $2 billion anti-weaponization fund and rewrite Trump's audit immunity language in a settlement agreement. Negotiations over those demands remain ongoing.

"The best thing is, take the win, get Blanche confirmed and get this agreement out of the way," Tillis told Fox News Digital.

When asked what it would take to get Tillis to vote to confirm Blanche, he said, "exactly what Blanche committed to."

TRUMP ADMIN PUSHES BACK ON 'SLUSH FUND' ATTACKS AGAINST ANTI-WEAPONIZATION FUND AND LAYS OUT WHO QUALIFIES

Tillis stressed that Blanche is not to blame for the impasse, saying he believes he "was honest" during his confirmation process and that he blames someone on Trump’s team.

"This is not Blanche's problem. It's clear to me that Blanche was honest when he answered without hesitation, working with us to end this," Tillis said.

"I believe that one of the president's advisors who were part of this agreement is the problem. And they need to own it."

Tillis also pointed out that there is no certainty that the Senate would be any more accepting of Blanche next year, particularly as Republicans have more seats in danger than Democrats in the Senate.

"The best-case scenario is you come back with the same number of people next year, and our members are not going to be any more supportive of this than they are today."

TRUMP-TILLIS TIFF DEEPENS AS PRESIDENT SAYS HE ‘QUIT,’ CONCEDES FED FIGHT COULD DOOM NEW CHAIR CONFIRMATION

Trump could still keep Blanche as acting attorney general for months even if he withdraws the nomination. The Federal Vacancies Reform Act allows acting officials to serve for 210 days, and withdrawing a pending nomination resets that clock. If Trump were to pull Blanche's nomination Thursday, Blanche could remain in the role until late February.

Despite Trump's public threat, Tillis said negotiations with the administration remain ongoing and said he is "not a no" on Blanche.

"In this place, nothing's ever as good or as bad as it seems, so we're continuing to negotiate," Tillis said.

Fox News Digital’s Alex Miller and Adam Pack contributed to this report.

item.title: Influencer accused of targeting wealthy dating app matches back behind bars
item.description: Adva Lavie, also known as Mia Ventura, allegedly cut her ankle monitor while awaiting trial on dating app burglary charges targeting wealthy victims.
item.content:encoded:
A Los Angeles influencer accused of targeting wealthy victims before stealing from them is back behind bars after authorities said she allegedly removed her ankle monitor while awaiting trial.

Adva Lavie, 28, who also goes by Mia Ventura, was arrested Tuesday night in Beverly Hills just months after she was released on electronic monitoring while awaiting trial on felony burglary charges.

Prosecutors said Lavie violated the conditions of her release by allegedly removing the electronic monitor she was ordered to wear. A judge has since revoked her release, ordered her held without bail and scheduled a bail review hearing for Friday in Van Nuys.

Court records also show Lavie was arrested on an outstanding Riverside County warrant in a separate grand theft case.

NEARLY 1 IN 12 DEFENDANTS ON ANKLE MONITORS IN CHICAGO HAVE GONE AWOL, AUTHORITIES SAY

Newly obtained court records show Riverside County prosecutors charged Lavie in April with felony grand theft after accusing her of stealing more than $11,000 in luxury items during the 2025 Coachella Music Festival.

Prosecutors said Lavie failed to appear for her scheduled May arraignment, prompting a judge to issue a $20,000 arrest warrant. As of Thursday afternoon, she had not yet been booked into Riverside County, and no in-custody arraignment had been scheduled.

HOMEOWNERS IN LEAFY ENCLAVES HIT BY BURGLARS ZEROING IN ON HIGH-END HOMES FOR SMASH-AND-GRAB SCORES

The Riverside case centers on allegations Lavie stole an approximately $8,600 Rolex watch, Louis Vuitton Aviator sunglasses valued at about $700 and a Louis Vuitton cardholder worth about $1,800 from a man she attended Coachella with.

Investigators said the man invited Lavie to stay with him at an Airbnb in Indio during Coachella weekend. After the pair argued, she allegedly helped herself to the luxury items from his unlocked Tesla Cybertruck before leaving.

According to an arrest warrant, surveillance cameras at the Airbnb captured the alleged theft, and detectives later identified Lavie from the video. Investigators also noted she was a suspect in another theft reported at the same property.

FLORIDA MAN WHO ALLEGEDLY LURED WOMEN WITH DATING APP COULD HAVE MORE VICTIMS: AUTHORITIES

Lavie's latest arrest comes nearly four months after Los Angeles County prosecutors accused her of carrying out a dating app burglary spree targeting wealthy victims across Southern California.

Prosecutors allege Lavie spent years using dating apps and "Sugar Daddy" websites to build relationships with wealthy older men and younger women before posing as a girlfriend or travel companion to gain access to their homes.

Once inside, authorities said, she stole cash, gold, credit cards and luxury designer items from victims in Westlake Village, West Hollywood, Los Angeles and Beverly Hills.

Lavie has pleaded not guilty to six felony charges, including two counts of grand theft, two counts of first-degree residential burglary and two counts of unauthorized use of personal identifying information. She was released from custody on an electronic ankle monitor before her latest arrest.

When announcing the case in March, Los Angeles County District Attorney Nathan Hochman said prosecutors intended to prove Lavie exploited the trust she built through online relationships.

"At her trial, we will prove beyond a reasonable doubt that this defendant exploited trust built through online relationships to gain access to victims' homes and steal from them," Hochman said. "Her ability to deceptively influence others, whether in person or online, has now come to an end."

The Los Angeles County Sheriff's Department previously released a public bulletin identifying Lavie as the suspect in the dating app burglary investigation and published photographs of luxury vehicles investigators said she drove, including a white Mercedes-Benz coupe and a black Porsche SUV.

Fox 11 Los Angeles previously reported that Lavie's fiancé, billionaire entrepreneur Stephen Cloobeck, was arrested on separate felony charges alleging he attempted to dissuade witnesses from testifying against her.

If convicted on all six felony counts in the Los Angeles County case, Lavie faces up to 11 years and eight months in state prison.

Fox News Digital's Michael Dorgan contributed to this report.

item.title: WNBA fans call out glaring double standard after Angel Reese’s clueless response to Paige Bueckers bet
item.description: Angel Reese said she'd be requesting her Apple Pay after the Dream's win over the Wings, brushing off criticism of her $400 bet with Paige Bueckers.
item.content:encoded:
Atlanta Dream star Angel Reese doesn't care about the PR damage control the WNBA is currently going through.

The WNBA was mercilessly criticized Wednesday after sharing, then deleting, a video featuring Reese and Wings player Paige Bueckers.

The league's social media team inadvertently highlighted one of the most sensitive issues in professional sports: gambling.

WNBA ADMITS CONTROVERSIAL BETTING VIDEO FEATURING ANGEL REESE, PAIGE BUECKERS 'MISSED THE MARK'

Reese and Bueckers agreed to a $400 bet ahead of Wednesday's matchup in Arlington.

After the Dream's narrow 82-81 win, Reese shrugged off the controversy when asked about the wager.

"Yeah, I’ll be requesting my Apple Pay after this," Reese said postgame.

WATCH:

Critics questioned whether this kind of "lighthearted" banter would ever fly in leagues like the NBA.

Others wondered whether Caitlin Clark and Sophie Cunningham would've received the same treatment. Just look at the firestorm surrounding Cunningham, then ask whether the sports media is holding Reese and Cunningham to the same standard.

EX-FORDHAM BASKETBALL PLAYERS PERMANENTLY BANNED BY NCAA OVER ALLEGED GAME MANIPULATION BETTING SCHEME

"[Reese] only admitted it because it was filmed, who knows what other games she bet on?" one critic wrote.

Another chimed in: "I wonder what the WNBA would have done if it was Caitlin Clark and Sophie Cunningham making a $400 wager on a game they are playing in instead of Angel Reese and Paige Bueckers?"

Under Section 5(c) of the WNBA's Collective Bargaining Agreement, players are strictly prohibited from placing wagers, directly, indirectly, or even as a side bet, on any league game. Violations give the commissioner broad authority to impose severe penalties, ranging from fines and suspensions to permanent banishment in order to protect the integrity of the league.

The post sparked immediate questions about potential violations of the league's anti-gambling policy, prompting the WNBA to release a statement addressing the deleted clip on Thursday (as reported by OutKick's Mark Harris).

The league characterized it as a "lighthearted exchange" and announced no discipline.

"While the social media post was intended to be lighthearted, WNBA players are well aware of the league's policies prohibiting betting on WNBA games and receive training every year reinforcing those policies," the statement read.

OutKick reached out for comment on its internal decision-making. We have not received a response.

"We recognized that the post missed the mark, removed it shortly after it was published, and addressed the matter internally. We will also use this as an opportunity to reemphasize with the players involved that conversations about wagering on WNBA games, even when intended as a joke, can have negative consequences."

Deleting the video solved an immediate public relations problem, but it also compromised the league's standard.

item.title: Mamdani's 'this is only the beginning' announcement cracking down on food delivery tips sparks outrage
item.description: New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani faced viral backlash Thursday over a post claiming responsibility for increasing food delivery service tips.
item.content:encoded:
New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani is facing fresh criticism after taking credit for a reported $104 million increase in delivery worker tips that critics say was made possible by legislation enacted before he took office and will likely only exacerbate cost of living issues in the city.

The criticism comes after Mamdani declared at a press conference Wednesday and in a social media post, "We've put $104 million back in delivery workers' pockets," citing changes to Uber Eats' and DoorDash's apps that made tipping more prominent.

"This is only the beginning," Mamdani wrote.

Those changes stem from a city law approved by the New York City Council before Mamdani became mayor. Former Mayor Eric Adams neither signed nor vetoed the measure, allowing it to become law after 30 days. The rules took effect in January under the Mamdani administration, which implemented and enforced the requirements.

MAMDANI'S 'RATION SHOP' GROCERY PLAN FACES BLISTERING ECONOMIC CRITIQUE AS OPPONENTS BLAST SOCIALIST POLICY

Before the law took effect, the New York City Department of Consumer and Worker Protection found that Uber Eats and DoorDash had hidden tip buttons and set default tips below 10%, contributing to a 79% decline in tips for delivery workers. The law required the companies to make tipping more prominent, and city officials say the resulting changes have since generated an estimated $104 million in additional tips.

Mamdani's office rejected the criticism that the mayor was taking credit for someone else's work, arguing that while the Department of Consumer and Worker Protection pushed for the reforms before he took office, the rules were implemented under his administration beginning Jan. 26. 

"A law is only as good as its implementation," a spokesperson for Mamdani told Fox News Digital. "We have been intentional about enforcing the laws on the books so that we are putting money back into the pockets of working New Yorkers."

Conservatives and political commentators on social media quickly blasted Mamdani for the already high costs of goods and services in New York City, and some accused the mayor of taking credit for legislation that was born before his term.
